title: Eukaryotic Cell Organelles
topicTitle: Detail structure of eukaryotic cells: cell wall, cell membrane, mitochondria, plastids, endoplasmic reticulum, golgi bodies, lysosomes, ribosomes, nucleus, chromosomes, cilia, flagella and cell inclusions
notes: **Cell wall (plants):** rigid outer layer of cellulose microfibrils embedded in pectin and lignin. Provides shape, protection and prevents over-expansion.
**Cell membrane:** phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. Fluid mosaic model. Functions: selective permeability, cell recognition, signal transduction.
**Mitochondria:** double membrane, inner membrane folded into cristae. Site of aerobic respiration. Contains its own DNA and ribosomes. Produces ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.
**Plastids:** chloroplasts (photosynthesis, contain thylakoids with chlorophyll), chromoplasts (pigments), leucoplasts (storage: starch, oil, protein).
**ER:** rough ER has ribosomes, synthesizes secretory and membrane proteins. Smooth ER synthesizes lipids and steroids, detoxifies drugs.
**Golgi bodies:** stack of flattened cisternae. Modifies, sorts and packages proteins for secretion or delivery to other organelles.
**Lysosomes:** membrane-bound vesicles containing hydrolytic enzymes. Digest worn-out organelles, engulfed pathogens and macromolecules.
**Ribosomes:** RNA-protein complexes, site of protein synthesis. 80S in eukaryotes (60S + 40S subunits), 70S in prokaryotes.
**Nucleus:** double membrane (nuclear envelope) with pores. Contains chromatin (DNA + histone proteins) and nucleolus (ribosome assembly).
**Chromosomes:** condensed chromatin during cell division. Each chromosome has a primary constriction (centromere) and two arms (p and q).
**Cilia and flagella:** 9+2 arrangement of microtubules (9 outer doublets + 2 central singlets). Cilia are short and numerous; flagella are long and few. Powered by dynein motors.

**Cell wall (plants) — detailed structure:** The primary cell wall is flexible and thin, composed of cellulose microfibrils cross-linked by hemicellulose and embedded in pectin polysaccharides. As the cell matures, a secondary cell wall may be deposited inside the primary wall, containing more cellulose and lignin for additional strength. The middle lamella (rich in pectin) cements adjacent cell walls together. Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels through the cell wall connecting adjacent plant cells for communication and transport.

**Cell membrane — fluid mosaic model details:** Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972). The phospholipid bilayer consists of phospholipids (glycerol + 2 fatty acid tails + phosphate group) arranged with hydrophilic heads facing outward and hydrophobic tails facing inward. Cholesterol molecules are interspersed between phospholipids, modulating membrane fluidity (prevents packing at high temperatures, prevents solidification at low temperatures). Integral proteins span the membrane; peripheral proteins are attached to the surface. The membrane is selectively permeable — small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) diffuse freely, while ions and large polar molecules require transport proteins.

**Mitochondria — detailed structure and function:** Mitochondria are double-membrane organelles: the outer membrane is smooth and permeable to small molecules; the inner membrane is highly folded into cristae, increasing surface area for ATP production. The inner membrane contains the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase. The matrix (innermost compartment) contains mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), 70S ribosomes, and enzymes for the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle). Mitochondria are the 'powerhouses of the cell,' producing ATP through oxidative phosphorylation: glucose is broken down to pyruvate (glycolysis in cytoplasm), pyruvate enters mitochondria, is converted to acetyl-CoA, enters the Krebs cycle, and the resulting NADH/FADH₂ feed electrons into the ETC, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis.

**Chloroplast structure and function:** Double-membrane organelle containing an internal membrane system of flattened sacs called thylakoids. Thylakoids are stacked into grana (singular: granum), connected by stroma lamellae. The fluid-filled space surrounding thylakoids is the stroma, containing enzymes for the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions), circular DNA, and 70S ribosomes. Chlorophyll and other photosynthetic pigments are embedded in the thylakoid membranes. Photosynthesis occurs in two stages: light-dependent reactions (in thylakoids, produce ATP and NADPH, release O₂) and light-independent reactions/Calvin cycle (in stroma, use ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into glucose).

**Endoplasmic reticulum — detailed functions:** The ER is an extensive network of membranous tubules and flattened sacs (cisternae) continuous with the nuclear envelope. Rough ER (studded with ribosomes) is the site of protein synthesis for secretory proteins, membrane proteins, and proteins destined for organelles. It also performs initial protein folding and glycosylation (addition of carbohydrate chains). Smooth ER (no ribosomes) synthesises lipids (phospholipids, steroids, oils), metabolises carbohydrates, detoxifies drugs and poisons (abundant in liver cells), and stores calcium ions (critical in muscle cells as the sarcoplasmic reticulum).

**Golgi apparatus — detailed structure and function:** Also called the Golgi complex or dictyosome. Consists of 4-20 flattened membranous sacs (cisternae) stacked like pancakes. Has a cis face (receiving side, near the ER) and a trans face (shipping side, facing the plasma membrane). Functions: receives proteins and lipids from the ER in transport vesicles, modifies them (glycosylation, phosphorylation, sulfation), sorts and packages them into vesicles for transport to destinations (lysosomes, plasma membrane, or secretion). Also synthesises polysaccharides for the plant cell wall and forms lysosomes.

**Lysosomes — detailed structure and function:** Single membrane-bound vesicles containing ~40 different acidic hydrolase enzymes (proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases, phosphatases) that function optimally at pH ~5. Formed by the Golgi apparatus. Functions: intracellular digestion of macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids), digestion of worn-out organelles (autophagy), destruction of engulfed pathogens (phagocytosis), and programmed cell death (autolysis when the cell is severely damaged). Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disorder where lack of hexosaminidase A leads to accumulation of gangliosides in nerve cells.

**Peroxisomes:** Single membrane-bound organelles containing oxidative enzymes (catalase, oxidase). Functions: break down fatty acids via beta-oxidation, detoxify toxic substances (especially in liver and kidney cells — convert H₂O₂ to water and oxygen via catalase), and in plant cells, participate in photorespiration (glyoxysomes in seeds convert fats to sugars). Unlike lysosomes, peroxisomes do not contain hydrolytic enzymes.

**Vacuoles:** Large membrane-bound sacs (tonoplast is the vacuolar membrane). In plant cells, the large central vacuole can occupy up to 90% of cell volume. Functions: stores water, ions, nutrients and waste products, maintains turgor pressure (critical for plant structure), contains pigments (anthocyanins in flower petals), and can contain hydrolytic enzymes (functionally similar to lysosomes in plants). Animal cells have smaller, temporary vacuoles (food vacuoles, contractile vacuoles in freshwater protozoa for osmoregulation).

**Nucleus — detailed structure:** The control centre of the cell, typically spherical and centrally located. Surrounded by the nuclear envelope (double membrane) — the outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER and studded with ribosomes. Nuclear pores (protein complexes called pore complexes) regulate transport between the nucleus and cytoplasm. The nucleoplasm contains chromatin (DNA wrapped around histone proteins). The nucleolus (1-3 per nucleus) is a dense region where rRNA is transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled. During cell division, the nucleolus disappears and chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes.

**Chromatin and chromosome organisation:** DNA in eukaryotic nuclei is organised as chromatin — DNA wrapped around histone proteins forming nucleosomes (beads-on-a-string structure). Each nucleosome consists of ~146 base pairs of DNA wrapped around an octamer of 8 histone proteins (2 each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4). H1 histone helps pack nucleosomes into thicker fibers. During cell division, chromatin further condenses into visible chromosomes. Human cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs — 22 autosomal pairs + 1 sex chromosome pair). Females: XX; Males: XY. Each chromosome has a centromere (primary constriction), two arms (p = short, q = long), and telomeres (protective caps at ends).

**Cytoskeleton:** A network of protein filaments that maintains cell shape, enables cell movement, and serves as tracks for intracellular transport. Three types: Microfilaments (actin filaments, 7 nm diameter) — involved in muscle contraction, cytokinesis, amoeboid movement, and maintains cell shape. Intermediate filaments (8-10 nm diameter) — provide mechanical strength, anchor organelles (e.g., keratin in epithelial cells, neurofilaments in neurons). Microtubules (25 nm diameter) — hollow tubes of tubulin protein, form the mitotic spindle, cilia, flagella, and serve as tracks for motor proteins (kinesin and dynein) transporting vesicles.

**Centrosome and centrioles:** The centrosome is the main microtubule-organising centre (MTOC) of animal cells, containing a pair of cylindrical centrioles (9 triplet microtubules arranged in a pinwheel pattern) surrounded by pericentriolar material. During cell division, centrioles duplicate and migrate to opposite poles to form the mitotic spindle apparatus. Plant cells lack centrioles but still form spindles. Basal bodies (structurally identical to centrioles) anchor cilia and flagella at the cell surface.

**Cell inclusions:** Non-living, non-membrane-bound substances stored in the cytoplasm. Examples: glycogen granules (carbohydrate storage in liver and muscle cells), lipid droplets (fat storage in adipose cells), pigment granules (melanin in skin cells, hemoglobin in red blood cells), secretory granules (enzymes in pancreatic cells, hormones in endocrine cells), and crystalline inclusions (some bacteria store polyphosphate crystals). These are not organelles but temporary storage deposits.

Lysosomes and peroxisomes are often confused: lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes (digestive enzymes) at acidic pH ~5 and break down macromolecules, pathogens, and worn-out organelles. Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes (catalase, oxidase) and break down fatty acids and detoxify harmful substances like H₂O₂ — they do NOT contain digestive enzymes.

Rough ER and smooth ER are often confused: rough ER has ribosomes attached to its cytoplasmic surface and is involved in protein synthesis, folding and modification (especially secretory and membrane proteins). Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification of drugs/poisons, and calcium ion storage (as sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle cells).

Cilia and microvilli are often confused: cilia are motile, hair-like projections containing a 9+2 microtubule arrangement covered by the plasma membrane; they move fluid or particles across the cell surface (e.g., respiratory tract). Microvilli are non-motile, finger-like projections of the plasma membrane containing only actin microfilaments (no microtubules); they increase surface area for absorption (e.g., small intestine).

Chromatin and chromosomes are the same material in different states: chromatin is the relaxed, uncoiled form of DNA-protein complex found during interphase (allows gene transcription). Chromosomes are the highly condensed, visible form of the same DNA-protein complex found during cell division. Human cells always have 46 chromosomes worth of DNA, but it is only visible as discrete chromosomes during mitosis/meiosis.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts share many features but have key differences: both have double membranes, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and reproduce by binary fission (supporting endosymbiotic theory). However, mitochondria are found in BOTH plant and animal cells and function in cellular respiration (breaking down glucose to produce ATP). Chloroplasts are found ONLY in plant cells and algae and function in photosynthesis (converting light energy to chemical energy). Mitochondria have cristae (inner membrane folds); chloroplasts have thylakoids (internal membrane sacs stacked into grana).

The nucleus contains the vast majority of a eukaryotic cell's DNA and serves as the control centre, directing protein synthesis and cell activities through gene expression regulation.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous organelles — they have their own DNA, ribosomes, and can replicate independently, but most of their proteins are encoded by nuclear DNA and imported from the cytoplasm.

The fluid mosaic model accurately describes membrane dynamics: phospholipids can move laterally within the layer (fluid), and proteins float within or across the bilayer (mosaic). Membrane fluidity is essential for cell function, vesicle formation, and cell division.

The endomembrane system (nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vesicles, plasma membrane) works as an integrated unit for protein synthesis, modification, sorting, and transport — demonstrating how cellular compartments are functionally connected.

Cell size is constrained by the surface area-to-volume ratio. As cells grow larger, their volume increases faster than their surface area, limiting the rate of material exchange. This is why cells divide rather than growing indefinitely, and why large organisms are made of many small cells rather than few large ones.
